# EP-457

## Problem Statement
Is there some $\epsilon>0$ such that there are infinitely many $n$ where all primes $p\leq (2+\epsilon)\log n$ divide\[\prod_{1\leq i\leq \log n}(n+i)?\]

## Site Remarks
A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Pomerance.

More generally, let $q(n,k)$ denote the least prime which does not divide $\prod_{1\leq i\leq k}(n+i)$. This problem asks whether\[q(n,\log n)\geq (2+\epsilon)\log n\]infinitely often. Taking $n$ to be the product of primes between $\log n$ and $(2+o(1))\log n$ gives an example where\[q(n,\log n)\geq (2+o(1))\log n.\]GPT-5.2 Pro (prompted by Barreto) has given a construction (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1b6puijShAt5hq3Vxnb45R0pm0WqVcJE8/view?usp=sharing) that gives an affirmative answer to the original question, with the constant $2$ replaced by $\frac{3}{\log 4}\approx 2.16$, and GPT later proved this with $2$ replaced by an arbitrarily large constant.

An elaboration sketched by Tao in the comments proves that there are infinitely many $n$ such that\[q(n,\log n) > \frac{1-o(1)}{2}\frac{\log\log n}{\log\log\log n}\log n.\]Tao suggests that standard heuristics suggest that this lower bound is also (up to constants) an upper bound for all $n$.

See also [663], and [1181] for upper bounds on $q(n,\log n)$.

- 18:12 on 02 Mar 2026 - TerenceTao (reply depth 1):
  The [Er79d] formulation is simply the negation of the [ErGr80] formulation. Here, I think this is simply a case where Erdos accidentally posed a problem that was too easy, because his initial explorations were not fully optimized.
  
  It is slightly more convenient to work with a symmetrized product $\prod_{-k/2 \leq i \leq k/2} (n+i)$ than the original product $\prod_{i=1}^k (n+i)$ (with now the very small technicality that $n$ has to be larger than $k/2$, which is easy to deal with, e.g., by forcing $n$ to be divisible by all primes up to $\log k$ or so). Roughly speaking, the challenge is to make this product divisible by every prime $p$ up to say $Ak$ for a large constant $A$, while keeing $n$ only as large as $\exp(k)$ at most.
  
  Primes up to $k$ automatically divide the product, so it is just the primes between $k$ and $Ak$ that cause an issue. In [Er79d] Erdos did the simplest thing of forcing $n$ to be divisible by all the primes between $k$ and $Ak$, which keeps $n$ under the size budget of $\exp(k)$ as long as $A \leq 2-o(1)$ by the prime number theorem. What GPT noticed was that one only needs $n$ to be within $k/2$ of being divisible by all primes between $k$ and $Ak$, which is a significantly more frequent event, and can be accomplished more cheaply using the Dirichlet approximation theorem: indeed one could achieve this with $n$ as small as something like $O(A)^{O(A k / \log k)}$, which stays under budget even if $A$ is as large as $\asymp \log k / \log\log k$. If I did the algebra correctly, this means that $q(n,\log n)$ can be as large as $\gg \log n \log\log n / \log\log\log n$ infinitely often (perhaps even $\geq (1-o(1)) \log n \log\log n / \log\log\log n$ if one does the accounting carefully). So the standard heuristics I mentioned back in September are in fact achievable as a lower bound! (Though proving that they are optimal -- i.e., providing the matching upper bound -- is likely to be extremely difficult, given how the much weaker bound posed in the commentary remains open.)
  
  The broader lesson here is that while Chinese remainder theorem methods can only force a number $n$ to obey various congruences mod $p$ for $p$ as large as $\log n$ or so, Dirichlet approximation theorem methods can control a larger range of moduli, but at the cost of only localizing $n \hbox{ mod } p$ to an interval rather than to a single value. For instance one can make $n \hbox{ mod } p$ within $\varepsilon p$ of the origin for all primes $p$ up to about $\log n \log\log n / \log \frac{1}{\varepsilon}$, I think, if $\varepsilon$ is not too small (for the application above one is setting $\varepsilon$ to be $\gg \log\log\log n/\log \log n$).
  
  The final problem of Erdos mentioned in the commentary (improving the trivial bound $q(n,\log n) \leq (1+o(1)) \log^2 n$ that arises from observing that the primorial of $q(n,k)$ clearly cannot exceed $\prod_{1 \leq i \leq k} (n+i)$) remains open though. I'll leave it to Thomas to decide whether to absorb it into the current problem (making it a two-parter), or spin it off as a separately numbered problem. It is a problem of a very different nature, having to do with ruling out long consecutive chains of nearly-smooth numbers, and likely comparable in difficulty to some of the other problems involving smooth (or powerful) numbers on this site.
  
  (The site has been updated to address this comment.)

## Local Computation
- direct finite profile for the least missing
 prime divisor q(n,k) of \prod_{1\le i\le k}(n+i).
- Observed large finite spikes in q(n,\log n)/\log n (max about 5.07 in
 range), with substantial finite densities above 2.
- Finite spikes do not settle the intended infinitude claim for a fixed
 2+\epsilon, but provide stronger empirical targets.

## Local Proof Attempts
Background gives a construction yielding
q(n,log n) >= (2+o(1)) log n for infinitely many n, where q is the least
missing prime divisor.

The strict improvement to (2+epsilon) log n is not proved by the cited
construction.

Target:
Upgrade known \(2+o(1)\) threshold to fixed \(2+\varepsilon\) infinitely often for least missing prime \(q(n,\lfloor\log n\rfloor)\).
A. Concrete Blocking Lemma (Most Critical):
Prove a prime-covering concentration lemma: for infinitely many \(n\), primes
\[
p\le (2+\varepsilon)\log n
\]
all divide \(\prod_{1\le i\le \log n}(n+i)\), i.e. residue classes of \(-i\) mod \(p\) are fully hit in the short interval.
B. Reduction Lemmas (with proofs):
Lemma B1 (least-missing-prime definition):
\[
q(n,k)=\min\{p\ \text{prime}: p\nmid \prod_{1\le i\le k}(n+i)\}.
\]
Proof.
Definition. \(\square\)
Lemma B2 (equivalence to full divisibility below threshold):
\[
q(n,k)>(2+\varepsilon)\log n
\iff
\forall p\le (2+\varepsilon)\log n,\ p\mid \prod_{i=1}^{k}(n+i).
\]
Proof.
By minimality in B1. \(\square\)
Lemma B3 (A implies infinitely-often claim):
If A holds for infinitely many \(n\) with \(k=\lfloor\log n\rfloor\), then \(q(n,\log n)/( \log n)\ge2+\varepsilon\) infinitely often.
Proof.
Apply B2 on those \(n\). \(\square\)
C. Main unresolved point:
The bottleneck is proving simultaneous small-prime divisibility across very short consecutive blocks with fixed positive margin above \(2\).
